findings.detail: The aging design guarantees no starvation once wait >= aging_window ONLY when (p_high - p_low) <= aging_max_bonus, because aging is capped. With defaults (aging_max_bonus=10) and the tested gap (5), at wait=100 low's effective (0+10=10) strictly exceeds any fresh high (5+0=5), so the C1 scenario is starvation-free regardless of tie-break. The cap is a configurable constructor knob; this bounded-bonus property is inherent to the stated design, not a defect.
findings.title: 'Never starved' guarantee is conditional on priority gap <= aging_max_bonus

findings.detail: At now=20 both demands have waited 20s, so aging=1 for each: urgent effective = 0+1+5 = 6, normal effective = 5+1 = 6 — a tie resolved by snapshot order (demand_id asc, urgent is pd-0). The urgency bonus is still decisive (without it urgent would score 1 < normal 5), and the acceptance outcome (urgent claimed, effective_priority==6) holds. Deterministic and correct; noted for accuracy.
findings.title: C2 urgency test outcome relies on deterministic tie-break, not a strict margin

findings.detail: The scheduler's ready filter and the additive claim(demand_id=...) branch check status and retry_at but not lease_until, unlike the default claim path. This is unreachable double-claim territory today because a leased demand always has status 'running' (rejected by the status check) — the ZR-507 lifecycle clears the lease on fail/complete/expire. Asymmetry worth documenting; not a current correctness issue.
findings.title: schedule_once/claim(demand_id) omit the lease_until check present in the default claim path

findings.detail: Replay shows low is claimed at t=50, where aging int(10*50/100)=5 ties the fresh high's 5 and snapshot order favors pd-0. The design guarantee is unaffected: at wait=100 the margin is strict (10 > 5), so low is claimed by t=50 at the latest and can never be starved in this scenario. The unit test passes as shipped.
